newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Yachting-Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: Australian Yachting-Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
NOT A GOOD WEEK FOR OCEAN SAILING

A week of extraordinary survival at sea but not such a great advertisement for international ocean yacht racing with the daily media focussing on the cost to the Australian taxpayer of the rescues from the Southern Ocean.

While Australia, and other nations around the world, have a responsibility under the Law of the Sea Convention to render aid to ships (and yachts) in distress, I agree with the Australian Maritime Safety Authority that it is foolhardy to allow single-handed racing yachts to sail so near to the Antarctic.

It may save the yachts in distance sailed but it also places them at even greater peril from violent winds and seas. What is also of concern in the Vendee Globe race is the number of yachts which have actually turned turtle, as well as breaking their rudders.
Rules of other round-the-world events such as the BOC Challenge solo race and the fully-crewed BT Challenge wisely prevent competitors from sailing at such low latitudes.

The question that hangs over the French-run Vendee Globe is the fact that competing yachts do not have to meet the strict construction guidelines of the American Bureau of Shipping, as do all yachts which sail in events such as the Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart.

Nevertheless, the series of search and rescue operations have given our defence forces a unique practical exercise, albeit at some cost. It is a tribute to the expertise of our RAAF and RAN personnel that these lone sailors have been rescued.

Unfortunately, such events can reflect on our own ocean racing events but again clubs like the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia can be proud of their strict application of international ocean racing safety rules. During the recent Hobart race, 17 yachts retired but only one required outside assistance to reach port and that was a short tow by a fishing trawler into Eden.
DOUBTS CAST OVER AUSTRALIAN WHITBREAD CHALLENGE

The shock resignation this week of ADRIENNE CAHALAN as skipper of Elle Racing has cast doubt over the future of Australia's first challenge for the Whitbread round-the-world race which starts from Southampton, England, next September.

Although it has been reported that the Elle Racing campaign will go ahead with the launching of the Western Australian-backed syndicate's new Whitbread-60 scheduled for Sydney this month, the withdrawal of CAHALAN and two other experienced members of the crew, helmsperson VANESSA DUDLEY and THERESA MITCH, certainly limits the crew experience.

CAHALAN was the only member of the crew with previous Whitbread experience and recently skippered the yacht on a training sail from Sydney to Hobart. She announced her resignation this week, after returning the yacht to Sydney, citing problems with funding and a restructuring of the project.

Although the syndicate, headed by JOHN HARVEY, has appointed U.S. America's Cup sailor JOAN TOUCHETTE as the new skipper, the challenge has lost much of its Australian enterprise with the departure of CAHALAN.
Meanwhile, the New South Wales government next week will formally announce Sydney as a second Australian stopover in addition to Fremantle for the 1997-98 Whitbread Race.

Apart from building the new Whitbread-60 for the Elle Racing syndicate, Sydney boatbuilder JOHN McCONAGHY has under construction a new W-60 for the British Silk Cut syndicate to be skippered by English yachtsman and former world champion LAWRIE SMITH.
YACHTING FOCUS ON PORT PHILLIP

Melbourne's vast Port Phillip which, in 1999 will host the world championship for nine of the 10 Olympic classes, will be the centre of Australian yachting over the next 10 days with the state's premier keelboat regatta, the Port Phillip Regatta, starting this weekend and the Sail Melbourne Olympic and International classes regatta starting next Tuesday.

The Port Phillip Regatta, now in its 19th year, has again attracted some 150 leading keelboats along with trailable yachts and the traditional couta boats for a week of highly competitive racing at various venues around the bay.

This year's regatta, organised by the active Victorian Yacht Council, has attracted some of Australia's best International Measurement System (IMS) racing yachts, including GIORGIO GJERGJA's Farr-47, Ausmaid, the overall IMS winner of the recent Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart, the 1995 Hobart race winner Terra Firma, a Murray-41, and the recently imported BZW Challenge, a Farr-designed Corel-45.

The clash between Ausmaid and BZW Challenge has added interest because BZW Challenge's owner, Sydney yachtsman RAY ROBERTS, is planning an appeal to the Australian Yachting Federation which, if successful, could cost Ausmaid her first place in the Hobart race.

ROBERTS is disputing the 33 minutes time allowance granted to BZW Challenge by the Hobart race jury after searching for a possible boat in distress during the Hobart race. ROBERTS had sought two hours redress, which would have ousted Ausmaid for number one place in IMS results.

Other prominent yachts competing in the Port Phillip Regatta include Sydney's famous maxi Condor and Atara and the local yachts, JLW Chutzpah, Seaview Challenge Again, Local Hero and the new Cape-35, Astrology.
The IMS fleet will sail two races tomorrow, Sunday and Monday, climaxing with the final race next Saturday from Portsea to Blairgowrie.
INTERNATIONAL SAILORS FOR SAIL MELBOURNE '97
Sailors from New Zealand, Japan, Germany, Singapore, China, South Korea and Guam will join the best of Australia's Olympic and International one-design sailors for Sail Melbourne '97.

MITCH BOOTH, Australia's bronze and silver medallist in the Tornado catamaran class at the past two Olympics, will head this spectacular class while Hong Kong's first Olympic gold medallist, LEE LAI-SHAN, will sail in the women's Mistral sailboard class.

LEE became a national hero in Hong Kong after her outstanding victory at the Atlanta Olympic regatta in Savannah and is now studying sports administration at the Australian National University in Canberra.

Other leading women boardsailors competing include New Zealand's BARBARA KENDALL, the Olympic gold medallist in 1992 and silver medallist in 1996, and Australia's Olympic representative and former world youth champion, NATASHA STURGES.

Sail Melbourne '97 has attracted a strong contingent for the Laser class, recently confirmed as the single-handed dinghy class for the Sydney 2000 Olympics, while entries for the Laser Radial class include former youth champions SARAH BLANCK and MELANIE DENNISON.
JOHN BERTRAND IN TOP FORM IN ETCHELLS

JOHN BERTRAND, the 1983 America's Cup-winning skipper with Australia II and the luckless campaigner at San Diego with oneAustralia, is back in the winners' list this week in the International Etchells, Australia's most popular one-design keelboat class.

After four heats, BERTRAND has sailed his well-named yacht, Two Saints and a Magpie (indicating the football allegiance of he and his crew), to 3-2-1-1 placings in the Australian championship being sailed from Adelaide's Royal South Australian Yacht Club.
This gives BERTRAND a net three points under the old Olympic pointscoring system after discarding one race.

His only real competition has come from Hobart's NICK ROGERS, sailing Karabos from The Royal Yacht Club of Tasmania. ROGERS, the former world champion in the Dragon class, has notched up a scorecard of 8-1-2-2 for a net six points.
* Peter Campbell is the editor of Offshore Yachting magazine.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800.
